passages.text: BLOOD, in anatomy, a red fluid, which circulates through the arteries and veins of animals, and is the immediate nourishment of every part of the body.
When drawn from a vein and suffered to rest, it separates into two parts: a red mass called the crassamentum, or cake, and a thin yellowish liquor named the serum.
The redness is owing to an infinite number of minute red globules, first discovered by the microscope of Leeuwenhoek, which swim in the serum and are thought to be compressible.
The blood is made from the chyle, which, being prepared from the aliment in the stomach and intestines, is conveyed by the lacteal vessels into the thoracic duct, and thence into the subclavian vein.
Its motion was first demonstrated by our countryman Dr Harvey, who shewed that the heart, by its contraction, drives the blood through the arteries to every part, from whence it returns by the veins.
Of the heat of the blood authors are not agreed; some ascribing it to a fermentation, others to the friction of its parts against the sides of the vessels.

The ancients reckoned the blood one of the four humours, and ascribed to its abundance the sanguine temperament. Physicians at this day relieve a plethora, or too great fulness of blood, by opening a vein.
The transfusion of blood from one animal into another was attempted in the last century both in England and France; but the experiments, having sometimes proved fatal, were forbidden by authority.

passages.text: Blood is a body fluid that delivers oxygen and nutrients to the cells and carries metabolic waste away from them. In vertebrates it is made up of blood cells suspended in plasma.

Plasma makes up about 55% of blood volume. It is mostly water and carries dissolved proteins, glucose, mineral ions, hormones and carbon dioxide. The rest is red blood cells (erythrocytes), white blood cells (leukocytes) and platelets.
Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, an iron-containing protein that binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues. Haemoglobin gives blood its red colour.
Blood cells are produced in the bone marrow, a process called haematopoiesis. Red blood cells circulate for about 120 days before the spleen and liver remove them.

The heart pumps blood around a closed system of arteries, capillaries and veins. The pulmonary circuit carries blood through the lungs, where it picks up oxygen; the systemic circuit carries it to the rest of the body.
When a vessel is injured, platelets and clotting factors form a clot. Strands of fibrin trap red cells into a solid mass, and the clear fluid left behind is called serum.
Heat is produced mainly by metabolism in the liver and muscles. Blood carries that heat around the body and helps keep its temperature stable.
Blood transfusion became routine after Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO blood groups in 1901. Matching the donor's group to the recipient's prevents fatal reactions.
Bloodletting, justified by the theory of the four humours, was common until the late 19th century. Today it is used only for a few conditions, such as haemochromatosis and polycythaemia.
Disorders of the blood include anaemia, haemophilia, leukaemia and sickle cell disease.

alignments.label: Blood circulates

britannica.quote: circulates through the arteries and veins

wikipedia.quote: a closed system of arteries, capillaries and veins

alignments.explanation: Both describe the same circuit. Wikipedia also names the capillaries that join arteries to veins.

alignments.label: The heart drives it

britannica.quote: the heart, by its contraction, drives the blood through the arteries

alignments.explanation: Harvey's account from 1628 still stands; only the wording is plainer.

alignments.label: Red globules
alignments.explanation: The same objects. "Globules" was the microscope-era name; they became "cells" once cell theory arrived in the 1830s.

alignments.label: The clot

britannica.quote: a red mass called the crassamentum, or cake

alignments.explanation: Crassamentum is Latin for "thickening". The observation is unchanged; the word has gone.

alignments.label: Serum

britannica.quote: a thin yellowish liquor named the serum

wikipedia.quote: the clear fluid left behind is called serum

alignments.explanation: Same word, same meaning, in both texts.

alignments.label: Where blood is made

britannica.quote: The blood is made from the chyle

wikipedia.quote: Blood cells are produced in the bone marrow

alignments.explanation: In 1797, blood is made from digested food. Today, food supplies the plasma, but the cells come from the bone marrow.

alignments.label: Why blood is warm

britannica.quote: some ascribing it to a fermentation, others to the friction of its parts

wikipedia.quote: Heat is produced mainly by metabolism in the liver and muscles

alignments.explanation: Neither 1797 theory survived. Heat comes from the tissues; blood only carries it.

alignments.label: Bloodletting

britannica.quote: relieve a plethora, or too great fulness of blood, by opening a vein

wikipedia.quote: Today it is used only for a few conditions

alignments.explanation: Routine treatment in 1797. Now kept for a few disorders where the body holds too much iron or too many red cells.

alignments.label: Transfusion

britannica.quote: having sometimes proved fatal, were forbidden by authority

wikipedia.quote: Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO blood groups in 1901

alignments.explanation: Right that it was dangerous, wrong about why: the deaths came from mismatched blood groups.

alignments.label: Blood and temperament

britannica.quote: ascribed to its abundance the sanguine temperament

alignments.explanation: The idea that blood shapes character has left medicine entirely.
